\sphinxstylestrong{Data quality:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Cells are kept only where the overall \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{QCflag}}, for value meaning see section {\hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:subpar-cmems-insitu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Copernicus Marine}}}}}, is equal to \(\{1,2,5,7,8\}\)(Copernicus In Situ Tac Data Management Team 2025)). Per\sphinxhyphen{}parameter flags (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CSPD\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DDNS\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GDOP\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VART\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POSITION\_QC}}) are retained but not used for filtering. QC flagging uses a maximum Geometric Dilution of Precision (GDOP) threshold and a maximum velocity for each radar, which are listed in Table \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}]{Table \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}}}. Any data point exceeding those values gets flagged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data quality:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Cells are kept only where the overall \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{QCflag}}, for value meaning see section {\hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:subpar-cmems-insitu}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Copernicus Marine}}}}}, is equal to \(\{1,2,5,7,8\}\)(Copernicus In Situ Tac Data Management Team 2025)). Per\sphinxhyphen{}parameter flags (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CSPD\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DDNS\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GDOP\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VART\_QC}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POSITION\_QC}}) are retained but not used for filtering. Five upstream tests, defined by the EU HFR Node’s own QC recommendations (Corgnati et al. 2024, Table 2), feed into the overall \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{QCflag}}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DDNS\_QC}} (Data Density Threshold) checks that at least a minimum number of three radial velocities contributed to the total\sphinxhyphen{}vector solution; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CSPD\_QC}} (Velocity Threshold) checks the total current speed against a region\sphinxhyphen{}specific maximum (see Table \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}]{Table \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}}}; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{VART\_QC}} (Variance Threshold or Temporal Derivative) checks the solution’s own temporal variance (only relevant for beam\sphinxhyphen{}forming systems); \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GDOP\_QC}} (Geometric Dilution of Precision (GDOP) Threshold) checks the GDOP against a region\sphinxhyphen{}specific maximum (see Table \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}]{Table \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-copernicus-hfr-resolutions}}}); and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{POSITION\_QC}} independently checks the solution’s own reported latitude/longitude, unrelated to the four velocity\sphinxhyphen{}based tests. Any data point failing at least one of the QC tests gets flagged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Availability:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Region\sphinxhyphen{}dependent. The near\sphinxhyphen{}real\sphinxhyphen{}time feed (last 30 days) is available for 19 of the 25 regions; the monthly feed (from up to 01\sphinxhyphen{}01\sphinxhyphen{}2020 \sphinxhyphen{} present (\(<30\) day latency)) and historic archive (typically large single file per radar) are available for all 25 regions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dataset acquisition:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Copernicus Marine near\sphinxhyphen{}real\sphinxhyphen{}time in\sphinxhyphen{}situ dataset (\sphinxurl{https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/INSITU\_GLO\_PHYBGCWAV\_DISCRETE\_MYNRT\_013\_030/description}; lastest (last 30 days) and monthly (from 01\sphinxhyphen{}01\sphinxhyphen{}2020) available), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{radar\sphinxhyphen{}total}} \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dataset\_part}}; delayed\sphinxhyphen{}mode currents dataset (\sphinxurl{https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/INSITU\_GLO\_PHY\_UV\_DISCRETE\_MY\_013\_044/description}), \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{radar\sphinxhyphen{}total}} product; both via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{copernicusmarine}} Python client (free registration).


\paragraph{NOAA \sphinxhyphen{} US radar coverage}
\label{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:noaa-us-radar-coverage}}\label{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:subpar-hfr-noaa}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Description:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Gridded, hourly total\sphinxhyphen{}vector surface\sphinxhyphen{}current fields (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{water\_u}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{water\_v}}) from the US Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS) National HF Radar Network (HFRNet), combined from individual radial\sphinxhyphen{}current sites and distributed by NOAA. The dataset is distributed via two different backends, ERDDAP griddap endpoint covering a rolling \(\sim\)90\sphinxhyphen{}day real\sphinxhyphen{}time window, and an NCEI THREDDS archive spanning 2006\sphinxhyphen{}present (latency of a few weeks). The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{l2o\sphinxhyphen{}qc}} toolbox tries the ERDDAP backend first, falling back to THREDDS for older dates the rolling window no longer covers. In case of no availability via NOAA, the Copernicus Marine HF radar database, as described in Section {\hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:subpar-hfr-cmems}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Copernicus Marine \sphinxhyphen{} global radar coverage}}}}}, is tried.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Characteristics:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A regular (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{time}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lat}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lon}}) grid at region\sphinxhyphen{}dependent resolutions of 0.5, 1, 2, or 6 km, at hourly cadence, across six regions: US West Coast, US East Coast/Gulf, Great Lakes, Hawaii, Puerto Rico/US Virgin Islands, and the Gulf of Alaska. See Table \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-hf-radar-res-noaa}]{Table \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-hf-radar-res-noaa}}} for available resolutions per region and retrieval mechanism. The locations of these regions can be seen in Figure \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:fig-hf-radar-coverage-us}]{Fig.\@ \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:fig-hf-radar-coverage-us}}} shows their bounding boxes).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data quality:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOAA’s HF\sphinxhyphen{}radar product carries no discrete per\sphinxhyphen{}cell QC flag on the delivered total\sphinxhyphen{}vector grid. Individual radials are filtered upstream before total\sphinxhyphen{}vector computation including among others a maximum\sphinxhyphen{}magnitude threshold, and a land mask (Otero 2021). Therefore, any value present in the retrieved data has already passed filtering.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Availability:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
ERDDAP: rolling \(\sim\)90\sphinxhyphen{}day window ending near real time. THREDDS archive: 2006 \textendash{} present (latency of a few weeks). See the per region availability in Table \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-hf-radar-res-noaa}]{Table \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:tab-hf-radar-res-noaa}}}. Together these archives cover a span of 2006 \textendash{} present for most of the regions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dataset acquisition:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP griddap server (\sphinxurl{https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/}); NOAA NCEI THREDDS HF\sphinxhyphen{}radar archive (\sphinxurl{https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/thredds-ocean/}); both public, no registration required.


\subsubsection{In\sphinxhyphen{}Situ Observations (Copernicus Marine)}
\label{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:in-situ-observations-copernicus-marine}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Description:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Dataset ID INSITU\_GLO\_PHYBGCWAV\_DISCRETE\_MYNRT\_013\_030, which contains in\sphinxhyphen{}situ observations. Relevant platforms reporting surface currents are buoys, moorings, drifters, and ferryboxes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Characteristics:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
point observations at native platform sampling rate; default collocation, which is user adjustable, is \(\pm\)30 min / 5 km aggregation radius.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data quality:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Real time quality control procedure subjects the currents (meta)data to 21 tests as described in the Copernicus Marine In Situ TAC quality control procedure (2025) (Copernicus In Situ Tac Data Management Team 2025). The resulting QC flag for current parameters, ranging from 0 \textendash{} 9, is the same as the one described in Section {\hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:subpar-cmems-insitu-waves}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Copernicus Marine}}}}}. Accepted QC flag codes are again \(\{1,2,5,7,8\}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Accuracy of current measurements are expected to be 0.5 \sphinxhyphen{} 1 cm/s (Wehde et al. 2025).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Availability:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Platform dependent, the Copernicus Marine dataset provides data from 1 January 2020 \sphinxhyphen{} present. Not all platforms measure surface currents. The geographical coverage of the platforms that do can be seen in Figure \hyperref[\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:fig-in-situ-currents-coverage}]{Fig.\@ \ref{\detokenize{05_reference_datasets:fig-in-situ-currents-coverage}}} for the first half of August 2026. Moorings have fixed locations, while the other platforms drift with the currents.

\centering
\capstart

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Dataset acquisition:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Copernicus Marine in\sphinxhyphen{}situ dataset (\sphinxurl{https://data.marine.copernicus.eu/product/INSITU\_GLO\_PHYBGCWAV\_DISCRETE\_MYNRT\_013\_030/}), download via the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{copernicusmarine}} Python client (free registration).

\subsection{Numerical Weather Prediction Ocean Calibration of SAR \protect\(\sigma_0\protect\)}
\label{\detokenize{alg-01-calibration:numerical-weather-prediction-ocean-calibration-of-sar-sigma-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The aim of the Numerical Weather Prediction Ocean Calibration (NOC)
({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-01-calibration:ref-verspeek-noc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Verspeek et al. (2012)}}}}}) is to provide an additional
calibration step to the SAR averaged normalized radar cross section
(\(\sigma_0\)) values used to retrieve the wind vector. These values are
generally averaged on a grid of a few kilometres (approximately
\(1\text{--}2 \times 1\text{--}2\ \mathrm{km}^2\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This calibration procedure is not applicable to sea\sphinxhyphen{}state parameters, since
these are derived spectrally. Therefore, an absolute \(\sigma_0\)
calibration is not necessary before retrieval. Instead, inter\sphinxhyphen{}calibration
among different sea\sphinxhyphen{}state parameter sources can be useful for comparison and
validation; this can be achieved with triple collocation (TC). Similarly, no
additional SAR\sphinxhyphen{}specific calibration procedure is recommended for line\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}sight
(LoS) current retrieval beyond the harmonized Doppler calibration already part
of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{l2o}} processor.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR \(\sigma_0\) values used to retrieve the wind\sphinxhyphen{}vector field.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Collocated wind vector from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Procedure}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set up approximately \(10^7\) NWP\sphinxhyphen{}wind/SAR\sphinxhyphen{}\(\sigma_0\)
collocations, to ensure that wind direction is sampled uniformly and that
the wind\sphinxhyphen{}speed range is adequately represented. Correct \(\sigma_0\)
for Faraday rotation, which arises from ionospheric propagation effects at
L\sphinxhyphen{}band and lower frequencies. Obtaining this many collocations requires
1\textendash{}2 months of acquisitions, depending on revisit frequency and coverage.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bin collocations by incidence angle, wind direction, and wind speed, with
bin sizes of \(1^\circ\), \(1^\circ\), and \(1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\),
respectively.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the expected (simulated) \(\sigma_0\) values using the
appropriate geophysical model function (GMF):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_{0}^{W,\mathrm{sim}}
= \mathrm{GMF}(\vec{u}^{\mathrm{NWP}}, \theta, f_c, \mathrm{pol})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\vec{u}^{\mathrm{NWP}}\) is the NWP wind vector, and
\(\theta\), \(f_c\), and \(\mathrm{pol}\) are the SAR incidence
angle, carrier frequency of the transmitted signal, and polarization
channel, respectively. The intended model is an L\sphinxhyphen{}band GMF (LMOD), analogous
to the CMOD7 GMF used for C\sphinxhyphen{}band SAR satellites such as Sentinel\sphinxhyphen{}1
({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-01-calibration:ref-stoffelen-cmod7}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stoffelen et al. (2017)}}}}}). The source marks
further LMOD specification as to be determined.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Obtain the final calibration\sphinxhyphen{}coefficient profile by weight\sphinxhyphen{}averaging the
ratios of simulated and measured \(\sigma_0^W\) values over wind
direction and then wind speed:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\alpha(\theta)
= \left\langle
  \left\langle
  \left\langle
  \frac{\sigma_{0}^{W,\mathrm{sim},ijk}(\theta)}
       {\sigma_{0}^{W,m,ij}(\theta)}
  \right\rangle_k
  \right\rangle_j
  \right\rangle_i .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\alpha\) is the calibration correction factor; \(k\) is
the index of occurrences in the \(\{i,j\}\) bin; and \(j\) and
\(i\) are the wind\sphinxhyphen{}direction and wind\sphinxhyphen{}speed indices, respectively. The
angle\sphinxhyphen{}bracket operator denotes the ensemble average.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Iterate the procedure until \(\alpha(\theta)\) is close to 1, according to
the selected threshold:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_{\alpha}
= \left|
   \frac{\sigma_{0}^{W,\mathrm{sim}}}{\sigma_{0}^{W,c}} - 1
  \right|
\leq \Delta_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{th}} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The corrected \(\sigma_0^W\) values are:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_{0}^{W,c}(\theta)
= \alpha(\theta)\sigma_{0}^{W,m}(\theta) .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In logarithmic space:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sigma_{0,\mathrm{dB}}^{W,c}(\theta)
= \alpha_{\mathrm{dB}}(\theta)
  + \sigma_{0,\mathrm{dB}}^{W,m}(\theta) .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metrics}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta_{\alpha}
= \left|
   \frac{\sigma_{0}^{W,\mathrm{sim}}}{\sigma_{0}^{W,c}} - 1
  \right| .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Outputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calibration coefficients: \(\alpha(\theta)\) (equivalently
\(\alpha_{\mathrm{dB}}(\theta)\)).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calibration residuals: \(\Delta_{\alpha}\).

\end{itemize}

\section{Validation}
\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation:validation}}\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation::doc}}

\subsection{Spatial Variance}
\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation:spatial-variance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Spatial Variance is a method used to estimate the representativeness error
\(r^2\), which is a key component for triple collocation (TC). This
procedure estimates the spatial variance for a given geophysical parameter.
Let \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) be two different sources characterized by
different spatial resolutions, where \(V_{s_1}(n)\) and
\(V_{s_2}(n)\) represent their spatial variances at spatial lag \(n\).
Given \(n_{\max}\), the maximum lag, the representativeness error of
\(s_1\) (the coarsest system) compared to \(s_2\) can be estimated as:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-r2-spatial-variance}
\begin{split}r^2 = \sum_{n=0}^{n_{\max}}
\left[V_{s_2}(n)-V_{s_1}(n)\right] .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\tilde{n}<n_{\max}\) be the spatial\sphinxhyphen{}lag threshold above which both
systems capture the same signal variability. The residual contribution then
vanishes:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}V_{s_2}(n)-V_{s_1}(n) \to 0
\qquad \forall n>\tilde{n} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Purpose}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method ({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:ref-vogelzang-spatial-variance}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Vogelzang et al. (2015)}}}}})
computes wind variances as a function of scale. Unlike the spectral\sphinxhyphen{}integration
method, it operates in the spatial domain rather than the frequency domain. It
is more tolerant to missing samples and provides a more intuitive
interpretation. The representativeness error is the difference between the
system 2 (e.g. satellite) spatial variance and that of system 3 (e.g. model).
This value depends on the selected scale. Spatial variances increase
monotonically with scale, and their difference also usually increases up to a
certain scale.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vector samples of the required geophysical parameter.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Procedure}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the first\sphinxhyphen{}order moments for both components of the geophysical
parameter of interest:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-spatial-first-moment}
\begin{split}M_{w,i}(n)
= \frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}w_{i+j} .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(w\) is the component of the geophysical parameter of interest,
\(n\) is the lag size, and \(i\) is an ancillary index identifying
the starting element.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the second\sphinxhyphen{}order moments:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-spatial-second-moment}
\begin{split}M_{ww,i}(n)
= \frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}w^{2}_{i+j} .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The subscript \(w\) denotes the first\sphinxhyphen{}order moment, while \(ww\)
denotes the second\sphinxhyphen{}order moment.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the spatial variance:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-local-spatial-variance}
\begin{split}V_{w,i}(n)
= \left\langle M_{ww,i}(n)-M_{w,i}^{2}(n)\right\rangle .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, angle brackets denote the expected\sphinxhyphen{}value operator.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average \(V_{w,i}\) to reduce uncertainty:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-average-spatial-variance}
\begin{split}V_w(n)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=0}^{M}V_{w,i}(n),
\qquad M=N-n .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Outputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(V_{u,v}(n)\).

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Triple Collocation}
\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation:triple-collocation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Purpose}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Triple collocation (TC) was conceived by Stoffelen (1998) as a tool for
inter\sphinxhyphen{}calibration and individual error assessment of three different
collocated sea\sphinxhyphen{}surface wind datasets
({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:ref-stoffelen-triple-collocation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Stoffelen (1998)}}}}}). TC is generic
and can be applied to any geophysical variable and data product, provided that
errors are additive, linear calibration is sufficient, measurement errors are
uncorrelated with each other, and measurement errors are constant over the
range of measured values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived wind products are recommended to be validated against buoy wind
measurements, scatterometer\sphinxhyphen{}derived winds, and NWP winds. Collocations between
SAR and scatterometers strictly depend on the Local Time Ascending Node (LTAN).
TC analysis needs a reliable estimate of the representativeness error
\(r^2\); see {\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:spatial-variance}]{\sphinxcrossref{Spatial Variance}}} for its estimation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inputs}

\sphinxAtStartPar
One or more triplets including the SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived parameter of interest. For wind,
the following sources are relevant:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived wind vector.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Scatterometer\sphinxhyphen{}derived wind vector.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Buoy wind vector.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NWP wind vector.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When available, buoy and scatterometer measurements are preferred to NWP
winds, due to their higher spatial resolution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For sea\sphinxhyphen{}state parameters such as significant wave height (SWH), relevant
validation sources are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived SWH.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Altimeter\sphinxhyphen{}derived SWH.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Buoy SWH measurement.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SWH from an NWP model.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For LoS surface currents, relevant validation sources are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived LoS surface currents.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
HF\sphinxhyphen{}radar total surface\sphinxhyphen{}current vector.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Buoy total surface\sphinxhyphen{}current vector.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
LoS surface currents from an NWP model.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Procedure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given three measurement systems, \(i=1,2,3\), representing, for example,
in\sphinxhyphen{}situ, satellite, and model estimates, the measurements and measurement
errors are approximated by the following linear expression
({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:ref-vogelzang-quadruple-collocation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Vogelzang and Stoffelen (2021)}}}}};
{\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:ref-vogelzang-quintuple-collocation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Vogelzang and Stoffelen (2022)}}}}}):
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-tc-linear-model}
\begin{split}s_i=a_i(t+\delta_i)+b_i .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(t\) is the common quantity, i.e. the true value of the parameter
at the scales commonly resolved by all three data sources. \(a_i\) and
\(b_i\) are the scaling and offset (bias) calibration coefficients,
respectively, and \(\delta_i\) is the random measurement error. For a
vector quantity such as wind, \(s\) can represent either the zonal
(\(u\)) or meridional (\(v\)) component. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Collocate triplets in space and time. For nominal wind regimes, the temporal
constraint should be less than 30 minutes and the spatial constraint within
25 km.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set the calibration reference data source (e.g. \(i=1\)), i.e.
\(a_1=1\) and \(b_1=0\) (e.g. in situ).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the variance common to these smaller scales,
\(r^2=\langle\delta_1\delta_2\rangle\) (representativeness error). See
{\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:spatial-variance}]{\sphinxcrossref{Spatial Variance}}} to compute \(r^2\), ensuring that \(s_1\),
\(s_2\), and \(s_3\) represent the higher\sphinxhyphen{}, intermediate\sphinxhyphen{}, and
coarser\sphinxhyphen{}resolution systems, respectively (e.g. buoys, satellite, and NWP
model).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the calibration coefficients iteratively until they satisfy a
selected convergence threshold.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calibrate the original measurements \(s_i^{\mathrm{uncal}}\) with the
new calibration coefficients:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_i=\frac{s_i^{\mathrm{uncal}}-b_i}{a_i},
\qquad \forall i\in\{1,2,3\} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is an inverse calibration. At the first iteration the scaling
coefficients are one and the bias coefficients are zero.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Apply the \(4\sigma\) test to exclude possible outliers.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the first\sphinxhyphen{} and second\sphinxhyphen{}order moments and the covariances using the
calibrated measurements for every combination of \(i,j=1,2,3\):
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-tc-moments}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
M_i &= \langle s_i\rangle, \\
M_{ij} &= \langle s_i s_j\rangle, \\
C_{ij} &= M_{ij}-M_iM_j .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the true common variance \(T\):
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-tc-true-variance}
\begin{split}T=\frac{C_{12}C_{13}}{C_{23}}-r^2 .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the calibration coefficients:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a_2=\frac{C_{23}}{C_{13}},
\qquad b_2=M_2-a_2M_1 .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a_3=\frac{C_{13}}{T},
\qquad b_3=M_3-a_3M_1 .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check convergence of \(a_{2,3}\) and \(b_{2,3}\):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\left|a_i^k-a_i^{k-1}\right|\leq10^{-6}\)
for all \(i\in\{2,3\}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\left|b_i^k-b_i^{k-1}\right|\leq10^{-6}\)
for all \(i\in\{2,3\}\), where \(k\) is the iteration index.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Iterate until convergence.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Estimate the measurement\sphinxhyphen{}error variances of the three sources:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-tc-error-variances}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_1^2 &= \frac{C_{11}}{a_1^2}-T-r^2, \\
\epsilon_2^2 &= \frac{C_{22}}{a_2^2}-T-r^2, \\
\epsilon_3^2 &= \frac{C_{33}}{a_3^2}-T .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metrics}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\left|a_i^k-a_i^{k-1}\right|\) for all \(i\in\{2,3\}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\left|b_i^k-b_i^{k-1}\right|\) for all \(i\in\{2,3\}\), where
\(k\) is the iteration index.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Outputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calibration coefficients: \(a_i,b_i\) for all \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Measurement\sphinxhyphen{}error variances: \(\epsilon_i^2\) for all
\(i\in\{1,2,3\}\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The error variances above are provided at the scale of the intermediate
resolution system (e.g. satellite). They can also be computed at the scale of
the coarser\sphinxhyphen{}resolution system (e.g. NWP model), using:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-tc-nwp-error-variances}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_{\mathrm{NWP},1}^{2}
  &= \epsilon_{\mathrm{SAT},1}^{2}+r^{2}, \\
\epsilon_{\mathrm{NWP},2}^{2}
  &= \epsilon_{\mathrm{SAT},2}^{2}+r^{2}, \\
\epsilon_{\mathrm{NWP},3}^{2}
  &= \epsilon_{\mathrm{SAT},3}^{2}.
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The labels SAT and NWP indicate the intermediate\sphinxhyphen{} and coarser\sphinxhyphen{}resolution
systems, respectively.


\subsection{One\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}One Validation}
\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation:one-to-one-validation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
One\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}one (1\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}1) validation assesses the SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived parameter against
individual reference sources through linear correlation analysis. This
approach is performed independently for each validation source, providing
direct pairwise comparisons between SAR observations and reference data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}one validation is particularly useful when TC is not feasible due to
insufficient collocated triplets. This may occur, for example, if the SAR
Local Time Ascending Node (LTAN) does not align with other altimeter or
scatterometer platforms and the region lacks in\sphinxhyphen{}situ sampling from buoys or
other point\sphinxhyphen{}based platforms. In such cases, validation against NWP models or
other available reference sources provides an essential quality assessment of
the SAR retrievals.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Purpose}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assess the retrieval performance of SAR retrievals against a reference
validation source.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Input}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
SAR\sphinxhyphen{}derived parameter.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NWP\sphinxhyphen{}model parameter or any other available validation source.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Procedure}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Collocate the two sources in space and time. A spatial constraint within
25 km and a temporal constraint within 30 minutes are recommended. For NWP
models, collect hourly forecasts if available; otherwise interpolate model
parameters bilinearly in space and time to the SAR wind\sphinxhyphen{}retrieval/vector cell
and acquisition time.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For circular variables such as wind direction, compute the differences
\(\Delta\phi\) and map the resulting angular differences to
\([-180^\circ,180^\circ]\):
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-direction-difference}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{raw}} &= \phi_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\phi_{\mathrm{VS}}, \\
\Delta\phi
  &= \Delta\phi_{\mathrm{raw}}-360^\circ
  &&\text{if }\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{raw}}>180^\circ, \\
\Delta\phi
  &= \Delta\phi_{\mathrm{raw}}+360^\circ
  &&\text{if }\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{raw}}<-180^\circ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute bias for all components.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute root mean square difference (RMSD) for all components.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For vector quantities, compute vector RMSD (vRMSD).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metrics}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Non\sphinxhyphen{}vector quantities:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bias: \(b=\langle VAR_{\mathrm{SAR}}-VAR_{\mathrm{VS}}\rangle\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(RMSD=\sqrt{\langle(VAR_{\mathrm{SAR}}-VAR_{\mathrm{VS}})^2\rangle}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pearson correlation coefficient:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r=
\frac{\left\langle
(VAR_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\overline{VAR}_{\mathrm{SAR}})
(VAR_{\mathrm{VS}}-\overline{VAR}_{\mathrm{VS}})
\right\rangle}
{\sigma_{\mathrm{SAR}}\sigma_{\mathrm{VS}}} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vector quantities (e.g. wind vector):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(b_w=\langle w_{\mathrm{SAR}}-w_{\mathrm{VS}}\rangle\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(RMSD_w=\sqrt{\langle(w_{\mathrm{SAR}}-w_{\mathrm{VS}})^2\rangle}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(vRMDS=\sqrt{\langle
(u_{\mathrm{SAR}}-u_{\mathrm{VS}})^2+
(v_{\mathrm{SAR}}-v_{\mathrm{VS}})^2\rangle}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pearson correlation coefficient:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}r_w=
\frac{\left\langle
(w_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\overline{w}_{\mathrm{SAR}})
(w_{\mathrm{VS}}-\overline{w}_{\mathrm{VS}})
\right\rangle}
{\sigma_{\mathrm{SAR}}\sigma_{\mathrm{VS}}} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Circular variables (e.g. wind direction):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(b_\phi=\langle\mathbf{mod}(\phi_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\phi_{\mathrm{VS}},360)\rangle\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(RMSD_\phi=\sqrt{\langle\mathbf{mod}(\phi_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\phi_{\mathrm{AS}},360)\rangle}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Jammalamadaka\textendash{}Sarma circular\sphinxhyphen{}circular correlation coefficient:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_c=
\frac{\left\langle
\sin(\phi_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\overline{\phi}_{\mathrm{SAR}})
\sin(\phi_{\mathrm{VS}}-\overline{\phi}_{\mathrm{VS}})
\right\rangle}
{\sqrt{
\left\langle\sin^2(\phi_{\mathrm{SAR}}-\overline{\phi}_{\mathrm{SAR}})\right\rangle
\left\langle\sin^2(\phi_{\mathrm{VS}}-\overline{\phi}_{\mathrm{VS}})\right\rangle
}} .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, angle brackets denote the expected\sphinxhyphen{}value operator, \(\mathbf{mod}\)
denotes modulus, and \(VS\) denotes validation source. \(VAR\) is the
validation variable of interest. Formulas with subscript \(w\) apply to
both components (\(u,v\)) and speed (\(U\)) for vector quantities.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Output}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Non\sphinxhyphen{}vector quantities:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bias: \(b\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(RMSD\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pearson correlation coefficient: \(r\).

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Vector quantities:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Bias for each component, speed, and direction:
\(b_u,b_v,b_U,b_\phi\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
RMSD for each component, speed, and direction:
\(RMSD_u,RMSD_v,RMSD_U,RMSD_\phi\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(vRMDS\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pearson correlation coefficient for each component and speed:
\(r_u,r_v,r_U\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Jammalamadaka\textendash{}Sarma circular\sphinxhyphen{}circular correlation coefficient for
direction: \(\rho_{c,\phi}\).

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Spectral Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{alg-02-validation:spectral-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Purpose}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Spectral analysis is a validation tool used to assess the spatial scales
resolved by the retrievals
({\hyperref[\detokenize{alg-02-validation:ref-vogelzang-spectral}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Vogelzang et al. (2011)}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M\) sets of \(N\) wind\sphinxhyphen{}component samples each, denoted
\(w_{ij}\), \(i=1,\ldots,M\), \(j=1,\ldots,N\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Procedure}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check for missing values in each set. Remove sets with missing values or fill
the gaps using an interpolation procedure.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute the power spectral density (PSD):
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-spectral-density}
\begin{split}\psi^{i}_{w,j}=\psi^{i}_{w,k_j}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\Delta}{N}\left|\hat{w}(k_j)\right|^2,
  & j=0\ \text{or}\ j=\dfrac{N}{2},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\Delta}{N}\left(
  \left|\hat{w}(k_j)\right|^2+
  \left|\hat{w}(k_{-j})\right|^2
\right),
  & j=1,\ldots,\dfrac{N}{2}-1,
\end{cases}
\qquad i=1,\ldots,M .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, \(\hat{w}\) is the Fast\sphinxhyphen{}Fourier transform (FFT) of the (vector)
component \(w\), \(\Delta\) is the spacing, and \(k_j\) is the
wavenumber.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average the PSD from each set:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-average-spectral-density}
\begin{split}\Psi_{w,j}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\psi^{i}_{w,j} .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PSD units are the squared units of the analyzed variable multiplied by the
spatial sampling interval \(\Delta\) (in metres). For wind components
and LoS surface currents, whose units are \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), PSD
units are \(\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-2}}\); for SWH, whose units are
\(\mathrm{m}\), PSD units are \(\mathrm{m^3}\).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metrics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In accordance with the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement
(GUM) Type A evaluation principles for spectral estimators, the standard
uncertainty \(u(\Psi_{w,j})\) of the averaged PSD is driven by the number
of independent scenes \(M\). Assuming a \(\chi^2\) distribution with
\(2M\) degrees of freedom for each spectral bin \(j\), the relative
standard uncertainty is:
\begin{equation}\label{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-psd-uncertainty}
\begin{split}\frac{u(\Psi_{w,j})}{\Psi_{w,j}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}} .\end{split}
\end{equation}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Outputs}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
PSD for each wind component: \(\Psi_{u,j},\Psi_{v,j}\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Associated standard\sphinxhyphen{}uncertainty profiles derived from
\eqref{equation:alg-02-validation:eq-cvtdd-psd-uncertainty}.

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Uncertainty analysis}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:uncertainty-analysis}}\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis::doc}}

\section{Introduction}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:introduction}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The “Evaluation of measurement data \textendash{} GUM” {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmgum}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}a)}}}}}, or the “GUM bible”, is a foundational international document that provides a conceptual and mathematical framework for identifying sources of uncertainty, quantifying them in a consistent way (as standard deviations), combining them into a single uncertainty figure, and reporting the result and its uncertainty clearly and comparably across disciplines and countries. Focusing on evaluation and expression of uncertainty in measurement it is an important component of the science of measurement and application, known as metrology (e.g., {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmvim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}b}}}}}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The GEO is an international partnership of governments and organizations acting as a policy and coordination body to promote global sharing and use of EO data, for example to support work on climate, disaster management, agriculture, water, and ecosystems. The GEOSS is the global, distributed infrastructure that GEO is building and coordinating. Rather than being a single system, it connects many independent EO systems \textendash{} such as satellites, ground networks, and ocean buoys \textendash{} from different countries and agencies, and aims to make them interoperable, accessible through common standards and interfaces, and accompanied by information about data quality and uncertainty. As such, GEO is the partnership, and GEOSS is the “system of systems” that GEO oversees.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To support its mission, GEOSS needs a metrological framework. As such, the 2010 endorsement of the QA4EO by the CEOS (part of GEOSS), has defined guidelines for EO applications based on principles adapted from the metrology community {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(Woolliams et al. 2025a)}}}}}. QA4EO aims to ensure that EO data are accessible, of known and documented quality, traceable to reference standards, in particular the SI, and suitable for user application (“fit for purpose”).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This section applies the GUM principles to SAR data and reviews the existing frameworks supporting metrology: the VIM {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmvim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}b)}}}}}, the GUM {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmgum}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}a)}}}}}, and QA4EO. The LaTeX source also refers to section labels for level\sphinxhyphen{}1, level\sphinxhyphen{}2, error propagation, and conclusions that are not defined there. Its product\sphinxhyphen{}specific uncertainty\sphinxhyphen{}estimation headings are retained below.


\section{The GUM Principles: A review}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:the-gum-principles-a-review}}

\subsection{The International Vocabulary of Metrology (VIM)}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:the-international-vocabulary-of-metrology-vim}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The International Vocabulary of Metrology (VIM; {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmvim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}b}}}}}) defines and organizes key concepts in metrology to ensure global consistency in measurement science. It provides standardized terminology covering quantities, units, and measuring instruments, with a focus on measurement uncertainty rather than error.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The document explains critical properties of measuring devices, such as precision, stability, and sensitivity, and highlights the importance of traceability and standards for reliability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Its applications span various fields, including physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and emerging areas like forensic science and food technology. Harmonization of terms is emphasized to ensure coherence in the various scientific, engineering, regulatory, and quality assurance fields.


\subsection{Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM)}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:guide-to-the-expression-of-uncertainty-in-measurement-gum}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The GUM establishes general rules for evaluating and expressing uncertainty in measurement that are intended to be applicable to a broad spectrum of measurements {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmgum}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}a)}}}}}. The guide was developed to solve the challenge of different laboratories and disciplines using different methods and terminology for uncertainty, which made measurement results difficult to compare.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The central idea of the GUM is to treat all components of uncertainty in the same mathematical way, regardless of whether they arise from random variation or systematic effects. Every component is represented by a probability distribution and a standard uncertainty. To obtain standard uncertainties, the GUM distinguishes between two kinds of evaluation. “Type A” evaluations use statistical analysis of repeated measurements, whereas “Type B” evaluations use all other available information, such as instrument specifications, calibration certificates, or expert judgment. The results of both evaluation types can be converted into standard uncertainties so they can be used on the same terms.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Measurements are described by a mathematical model that links the quantity being measured (the measurand) to various input, or influence, quantities. Once standard uncertainties of the influence quantities are estimated, they are combined \textendash{} taking into account any correlations \textendash{} using standard rules for propagating variances. This yields the combined standard uncertainty of the measurand, taken as the estimated standard deviation associated with the result. An expanded uncertainty is obtained by multiplying the standard uncertainty by a coverage factor \(k\). The purpose of the expanded uncertainty is to provide an interval about the result of a measurement that may be expected to encompass a large fraction of the distribution of values that could reasonably be attributed to the measurand. The value of \(k\) and how it was chosen must always be stated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A key emphasis of the GUM is transparency. An uncertainty statement should clearly describe which inputs were considered, how each uncertainty component was obtained, what assumptions were made, and how the components were combined. The document supplements this framework with definitions, statistical background, guidance on practical evaluation, and worked examples. In doing so, it provides a common language and method that allow measurement results and their uncertainties to be understood and compared across borders and domains.


\subsection{Quality Assurance Framework for Earth Observation (QA4EO)}
\label{\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:quality-assurance-framework-for-earth-observation-qa4eo}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
GEOSS depends on interoperable and quality\sphinxhyphen{}assured data to derive comprehensive information about climate and environment, as well as, e.g., food, water and energy security. To achieve interoperability across systems and datasets, common and well\sphinxhyphen{}defined data and metadata formats are needed, but also metrological principles such as traceability to SI, documented uncertainty analysis and comparison between different measurement references must be followed, and are key to the QA4EO reports {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo1}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(Woolliams et al. 2025a)}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Beside {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmvim}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}b}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-jcgmgum}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{BIPM et al., n.d.\sphinxhyphen{}a}}}}}, QA4EO also builds on EO\sphinxhyphen{}metrology collaboration in the EU FP7 and Horizon 2020, ESA and Copernicus projects and, in particular, the FIDUCEO project {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-mittaz19}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(Mittaz et al. 2019)}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As summarized in {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(Woolliams et al. 2025b)}}}}}, three basic metrology principles generally apply to EO data:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Traceability:} Metrological traceability is a property of a measurement that relates the measured value to a stated metrological reference through an unbroken chain of calibrations or comparisons. It requires, for each step in the traceability chain, that uncertainties are evaluated and that methodologies are documented.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty Analysis:} Uncertainty analysis is the review of all sources of uncertainty and the propagation of that uncertainty through the traceability chain. It is based on the suite of documents prepared by the JCGM and together known as the GUM.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Comparison:} Metrologists validate uncertainty analysis and confirm traceability through comparisons. The Mutual Recognition Arrangement (a formal arrangement to confirm the degree\sphinxhyphen{}of\sphinxhyphen{}equivalence between SI realisations and disseminations in different countries) requires regular, formal international comparisons that are conducted under strict rules.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The uncertainty analysis, as outlined in the GUM, should follow these principles.

\sphinxAtStartPar
ESA has initially applied the terms FRM, FDR and TDP to describe metrologically rigorous observations of specific relevance to space\sphinxhyphen{}based observations {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{(Woolliams et al. 2025b)}}}}}. The terms are increasingly being used by the broader EO community, although they have not yet been formally endorsed. The terms are defined in {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Woolliams et al. 2025b}}}}}, as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fundamental Data Record (FDR):} An FDR is a record, of sufficient duration for its application, of uncertainty\sphinxhyphen{}quantified sensor observations calibrated to physical units and located in time and space, together with all ancillary and lower\sphinxhyphen{}level instrument data used to calibrate and locate the observations and to estimate uncertainty.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Thematic Data Product (TDP):} A TDP is a record, of sufficient duration for its application, of uncertainty\sphinxhyphen{}quantified retrieved values of a geophysical variable, along with all ancillary data used in retrieval and uncertainty estimation.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fiducial Reference Measurement (FRM):} An FRM is a suite of independent, fully characterised, and traceable (to a community agreed reference, ideally SI) measurements of a satellite relevant measurand, tailored specifically to address the calibration/validation needs of a class of satellite borne sensors and that follow the guidelines outlined by the GEO/CEOS QA4EO.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As highlighted by {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo2}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Woolliams et al. 2025b}}}}}, “TDPs provide higher level products that have been processed from FDRs, through algorithms which also often combine information from other FDRs (e.g., from other satellite sensors) or from external information (such as reanalysis models and/or certain non\sphinxhyphen{}satellite data), along with such additional information”. Guidelines for assessing observational systems with respect to FRMs have been established by CEOS.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to establish a systematic process for generating uncertainty budgets, and ensuring that EO data are interoperable, temporally stable, and fit for scientific, operational and decision\sphinxhyphen{}making purposes, the QA4EO and EO projects acknowledged in {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Woolliams et al. 2025c}}}}} have adapted the stages, suggested in GUM, required to support the development of a measurement model and from that an uncertainty analysis. These EO specific stages of uncertainty analysis are given by {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Woolliams et al. 2025c}}}}} as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 1: Define the measurand and measurement model.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 2: Establish the traceability with a diagram.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 3: Evaluate each source of uncertainty and fill out an effects table.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 4: Calculate the data product and uncertainties.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Step 5: Record information about the uncertainty analysis for long term data preservation purposes and summarise for today’s users.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These steps are discussed in detail in {\hyperref[\detokenize{04_uncertainty_analysis:ref-qa4eo3}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-ref}{Woolliams et al. 2025c}}}}}. The product\sphinxhyphen{}specific headings below retain the source’s intended level\sphinxhyphen{}1 and level\sphinxhyphen{}2 uncertainty\sphinxhyphen{}estimation scope.
